q: I’m new to this. What is the originary hypothesis, and why does it matter?
a:
## The hypothesis in brief

The originary hypothesis was put forward by Eric Gans in *The Origin of Language* (1981). It is a hypothesis about a single event in which language, the human community and the sacred all began together. Katz takes it as the starting point of Center Study, and in *Anthropomorphics* he summarises it this way: it "posits a singular event within which language, or the sign, originates" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-1)).

The scenario has four steps.

1. **Imitation.** Humans, and the hominids just before us, are the most imitative of creatures. We learn what to want by watching what others want. Katz thinks this needs little argument: "how could anything we do, say or think not be composed of words and/or gestures that we acquired mimetically?" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-3)).

2. **Rivalry.** Imitation produces rivalry, because if I want what my model wants, he becomes my obstacle. Picture a group of proto-humans around a carcass. Ordinarily the pecking order settles who eats first. On this occasion, mimetic intensity overrides it and everyone converges at once. "Appetite becomes 'desire,' that is, a social phenomenon involving one's relation to others and not merely the object itself" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-4)).

3. **The sign.** At the brink of a free-for-all, "some member hesitates, presumably out of something like terror… is seen by others to hesitate, and is imitated by others. The gesture indicates a renunciation, perhaps momentary (but that is enough), of the desired object. This, what Gans calls 'the gesture of aborted appropriation,' is the first sign" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-5)). A grasping hand becomes a pointing hand. The same capacity for imitation that was driving the group toward violence now spreads a gesture that holds it off.

4. **The sacred center.** Nobody on that scene could think "I decided to stop." What holds them back seems to be the object itself. So "the creation of the human is mediated by the creation of the sacred center as the creator of the human" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-6)).

The core formula of the field follows from this: **representation is the deferral of violence.** "Deferral" is a precise word here. The sign does not abolish the danger. It postpones it, making it, in Katz's phrase, "imminently imminent," which "gives us a little space within which to work" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-4)).

Gans built this partly by correcting René Girard, who had placed a collective lynching at the origin of the human. Gans's objection was that a killing alone would not be memorable without a sign, and once the sign does the work, the killing becomes unnecessary ([Generative Anthropology as the One Big Discipline](/post/generative-anthropology-one-big-discipline#p-15)).

## Why it matters

**It answers a question nothing else answers well.** How can people point at something together and agree that it is "the same thing," using sounds that have no necessary tie to what they mean? Katz argues "there's simply no other way to account for the simple fact that humans can point to something and affirm that it is the same thing" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-3)). A gradual biological story leaves out the threshold where meaning appears. Shared, conventional meaning seems to require a scene where it was first shared, "How could language have emerged other than in an event?" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-6)).

**It is minimal.** "All it really assumes is that human beings are mimetic creatures" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)). From that one assumption you get language, the sacred, ritual and resentment, the feeling directed at whatever, ultimately the center, blocks our desire.

**It gives a working definition of the human.** On this account, the human is "the only species… that poses a greater danger to its own survival than is posed to it by anything in its environment" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-5)). Every institution then becomes legible as a way of holding that danger off.

**The scene never closed.** This is Katz's strongest claim, and it is where the hypothesis becomes a way of thinking rather than a story about prehistory. Each later scene inherits the task of the first, so "you are, literally, on the originary scene itself, which has never been 'closed,' only sustained and suspended, and … the very next thing you say will be version of the originary gesture that keeps the event in play or a premature attempt at appropriation that will collapse the scene" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-8)). Ritual, law, money, politics and technology all become versions of the original gesture.

**There is always a center.** Whatever we gather around, whether a sacred object, a king or a meeting's chair, organizes us. Katz develops this into his whole account of power and succession (in brief: how authority is handed on). "Can we even converse without focusing on someone, who thereby becomes the center of our deliberations?" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-14)).

## Trying it on something ordinary

Picture a meeting where three people start talking at once. The scene is about to collapse into noise and irritation. Then one of them stops, opens a hand toward another, and says "go ahead." That is a small aborted appropriation: a move toward the floor turned into a gesture that hands it over. It works because the others can imitate it, so turn-taking appears. If the meeting has a chair, the gesture has been made into an institution, and the chair now occupies the center that settles who speaks. Katz has a phrase for what this achieves: "everyone saying the same thing so that everyone doesn't do the same thing at the same time" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-19)).

## The status of the claim

The hypothesis can never be proven. No evidence of the event could survive. Katz still insists it "is to be taken literally and seriously," and that it is also "an answer to a very basic, inevitable question—why do words 'mean'?" ([Language, the Deepest and Most Reliable Tradition](/post/language-the-deepest-and-most-reliable-tradition#p-15)). He admits that accepting it can feel "something like a conversion experience," because you have to rethink your earlier assumptions from the ground up ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)).

## What to read next

- [Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic) and [Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence). These are short spoken pieces that unpack the two engines of the hypothesis, imitation and deferral.
- [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself). This is Katz's candid account of what the hypothesis asks of you and why people resist it.
- Later, [Addressing an Objection to the Originary Hypothesis](/post/addressing-an-objection-to-the-originary-hypthesis). Here Katz answers a serious critic, which is the best way to see where the scenario is under pressure.

**An exercise:** pick any rule or custom you follow without thinking, such as queueing, saying "excuse me," or waiting for the host to start eating. Ask what rivalry it heads off. Then ask what object or position sits at the center that everyone is deferring to.

q: What does Center Study mean by “the center”?
a:
The short answer is that the center is whatever holds a group's shared attention. It is also, more or less, the whole of Center Study. To see why the word carries so much, start with the scene where Katz says it first appears.

## Where the center comes from: the originary scene

The starting point is the originary hypothesis. A group of not-yet-human hominids converge on one desired object, say a fresh kill. Imitation intensifies their desire until the old pecking order breaks down. Then someone's grasping movement falters into a gesture, the others imitate it, and the rush is deferred. That faltered grasp is the first sign.

What matters for your question is what the object turns into at that moment. Katz writes that the only agency that could seem to be holding the group back is the object itself, and so "The creation of the human is mediated by the creation of the sacred center as the creator of the human" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-6)).

The center is therefore not just the thing in the middle. It is the thing as it has been made significant by everyone's shared, deferred attention. His most compact definition:

> "What is a center? Whatever can invoke and be referenced by an ostensive sign: the center is both cause and product of the sign—as cause it subsists beyond any particular reference, and as product it is continually renewed." ([The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center#p-1))

"Ostensive" means the pointing kind of sign, the "look, that." So whenever we can point at something together and know that we are pointing together, there is a center. And the center outlasts any particular object placed in it: the kill gets eaten, but the place where it was, and what it meant, remains.

## Attention before intention

This is why Katz replaces the philosopher's starting point. Most theory begins with subjects who intend, or with objects governed by laws. Center Study begins "with a center that compels" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-4)). The compulsion is very basic: "it holds you: while you're looking at it you're not looking away," and since others are looking too, "the center creates the margin, so you're looking at others on the margin as held by the center, just as you are" ([p-5](/post/the-center#p-5)).

So your relation to other people always runs through a third thing. Katz pushes this as far as it can go: "all of our thoughts and deeds are of the center—commanded by the center, carried out for the benefit of the center." He prefers to call our responsiveness a "hearing" of the center rather than a "reading", "because you hear whether you want to or not" ([p-6](/post/the-center#p-6)).

## The center comes before the self

A consequence that newcomers often find surprising is that the center is a source of agency before we are. "It is the center, first of all, that has agency—human agency will later come to be modeled on the agency of the center" ([The Center and the Declarative](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-the-declarative#p-19)). This is what the name *Anthropomorphics* points to. Humans gave the center wants, moods and commands before they thought of themselves in those terms, and then modeled themselves on it.

Katz is also careful not to reduce the center to a projection of individuals added together. It is "the collective or aggregate signifying capacities of the community," but those capacities "are only real in their collective and aggregated form" ([same text, p-14](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-the-declarative#p-14)). This is a deliberate break from humanism: "in place of the divine or holy we have the center which can never quite be 'human' yet governs all. There is a relation to the center, not a human essence present in each individual" ([Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human#p-5)).

## Two centers: signifying and occupied

Here Center Study turns political. History changes when a person takes the place of the sacred object. "The first revolution in human affairs was some individual 'seizing' the center—what the anthropologists call the Big Man, and from whom follow (along extremely complicated routes) all the kings and emperors and prime ministers and presidents and even 'bosses'" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-16)).

From that point there are two centers to keep apart. The **signifying center** is the sacred, the meaning-giving locus that subsists beyond any occupant. The **occupied center** is whoever actually holds the position and distributes. In Katz's words: "there's the center, and there's centrality, or, as I've called it, the occupied center and the signifying center. And the first thing the center tells or commands us is to sustain centrality" ([Lecture 4](/post/the-center#p-6)).

Much of modern disorder, on his account, lives in the gap between the two: "One's place in relation to the signifying center is fundamentally questionable, even if one's relation to the occupied center is not—hence the discrepancy" ([Talk of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-talk-of-the-center#p-1)). This is why succession matters so much in his later work. Handing the occupied center from one holder to the next is how continuity with the signifying center is kept or lost.

## There is always a center

You might ask whether we couldn't do without one. Katz's answer is that every attempt to do so just installs another center. Whoever claims to have debunked an authority "will necessarily put another centrality in its place," whether that is "facts," "reason," "rights" or "faith" ([Lecture 4](/post/the-center#p-13)). Even a free association with no boss has someone who "takes the initiative, someone sets the tone," and so "there must always be a center, even if the forms 'centering' might take are infinite" ([Prospects](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-17), [p-17](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-17)).

This also reframes the emotions. "All resentment is toward the center, and yet it seems like we're really resenting the guy next to us" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-15)). The counterpart is what Katz calls originary debt, "unending gratitude toward the center, in whatever form the center might take" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-24)). His slogan "donate your resentment to the center" follows from this. Bring a grievance back to the question of what the center has commanded and failed to secure, instead of spending it on the person beside you.

## Trying it out

Take any conversation you were in this week. Katz asks: "Can we even converse without focusing on someone, who thereby becomes the center of our deliberations, weighed down by our projections and myth-making?" ([Prospects](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-14)). Work through three questions about it:

1. What, or who, held everyone's attention?
2. Who set the tone, so that for a moment they occupied the center?
3. What did the center "command": which moves were possible, and which would have broken up the scene?

If there was friction, ask whether the resentment was really toward the person you were annoyed with, or toward whatever was supposed to keep things fair and didn't.

## What to read next

- **[Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center)** is the clearest single statement. It covers attention versus intention, signifying versus occupied center, and the exemplary victim, and it ends with what "the command of the center" means today.
- **[The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center)**, followed by **[Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center)**, both from *Anthropomorphics*. Together they lay out how leadership, power and succession grow from the originary center.

A question to take further: if every debunking installs a new center, what is the center of Center Study itself, and what would it mean for it to be a good one?

q: What does Center Study have to say about money and debt?
a:
Katz's answer comes in one sentence, which is also the title of the essay he wrote with Zack Baker: *There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center*. Money, credit, markets and capital are not a separate domain with its own laws. They are late forms of an obligation that begins on the originary scene. The rest is working out what that claim implies.

## Originary debt

Start with the originary scene. A group converges on a desired object, the convergence is arrested by a gesture of deferral, and the object becomes a center that gives the group its existence and its meal. That exchange is lopsided from the start: the center gives first, the periphery answers. Katz writes:

> "That humanity is constituted in debt to the center is, first of all, a consequential enough thesis to dwell on a bit." ([Data as Currency and the Debt to the Center](/post/data-as-currency-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-1))

The lopsidedness, "with the center first giving and those on the periphery then responding in kind, makes talk of debt unavoidable." Sacrifice is the first form of payment: "humans have always acknowledged a debt to the center—otherwise, what were all those sacrifices about?" ([Urbanomics](/post/urbanomics#p-11)).

At its most compressed, "debt is the tokenization of deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). Every share you receive is a gift from the center, and taking it in the sanctioned way is how you pay down what you owe.

## Money as credit drawn on the center

Gans once argued that the instantaneous market exchange, coins for coffee with the debt settled at once, breaks with the originary scene and becomes only a "minimal model" of it. Katz and Baker reject this: "the commercial transaction is, indeed, an extension of the originary scene" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-6)). They keep Gans's own phrase for money, "a credit drawn on the sacred," and read it as "a continuation of the originary debt we owe the center" ([p-19](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-19)).

Historically, drawing on Christine Desan, money starts as a receipt the king issues for contributions made ahead of time: "Money records, by the center, a debt paid to the center, and that record can in turn become a way of paying debts to the center" ([p-36](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-36)). General commerce grows out of these receipts, but always "through reference, however indirect, to the center." Hence the formula in *Anthropomorphics*: "money is a form taken by the delegation of power, and is therefore a form of power itself" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-18)). Following Samuel Chambers, Katz adds that "all money is credit—any token refers to a creditor and debtor." In the end "a chain of credit ultimately winds its way back to the state" ([On Credit and the Idiom](/post/on-credit-and-the-idiom#p-6)).

This is also where he parts from David Graeber. Graeber finds an unpayable debt obscene and imagines a debt-free community at the origin. For Katz that imagined community is exactly what the originary hypothesis rules out.

## The modern settlement: the outside spread and the outside option

Katz places the decisive break in late 17th-century England, with the Bank of England and the first two-party rotation. He borrows two terms from Colin Drumm. The **outside spread** is the lender of last resort. The **outside option** is "whoever within a monarchical order might be leveraged as a possible replacement to the king" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-1)). The English settlement "internalized both": the bank took over funding, and party rotation absorbed the replacement of the ruler. As a result, "the rotation system is tethered to the fluctuations of debt and repayment" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-2)).

Two consequences follow.

First, the modern state is "ultimately a debt enforcement institution" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-50)), and politics becomes a fight over whose debts get enforced and whose forgiven.

Second, credit and succession become fused: "a healthy, which is to say reliable and predictable credit system is necessary for orderly succession, while, conversely, disrupting the credit system is a good way of interfering with succession" ([Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession#p-6)). Katz notes, drawing on Wennerlind, that journalism was born from each party trying to damage credit while the other held power.

What modernity adds to the originary debt is the measure: "the value of our debt is determined by expectation of future earnings" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)). That is Bichler and Nitzan's *Capital as Power* read through the center.

There is a sharper, critical point as well. Where command is clear, a superior can hold you directly to account. Debt appears where that clarity is missing: "What debt, and ultimately money, do... is represent hedges against direct accountability" ([Discipline and Debt](/post/discipline-and-debt#p-5)).

## Enforcement and forgiveness: the juridical

If money is credit, then ruling largely comes down to deciding which debts to enforce and which to forgive. Katz goes so far as to say that "determining debt enforcement and forgiveness might simply be a definition of the juridical" ([Toward a Curriculum](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-23)). His working maxim is: "you forgive what has happened and enforce what one has done" ([Debits and Credits](/post/debits-and-credits#p-19)). Criminal punishment falls under the same heading as debt enforcement. The ancient jubilee, in his reading, was a periodic restoration of clear chains of command, not an anarchist impulse.

## The horizon: beyond money

Because money hedges against a center that cannot guarantee its own succession, the remedy Katz proposes is to make succession secure and let money wither. "The thinking of singularized succession, then, must involve thinking the abolition of money" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-2)). Money is already a form of data, so exchange could move toward data exchange with the center, toward "pedagogical futures," and toward idioms as currency: "Very explicitly, I want words and other signs to replace money, the debt to the center to replace monetary debt" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-12)). The practical first step is institutional: "Capitalism can only be transcended by forming companies which discount against expected future earnings foundationally, by charter, beyond the life span of anyone running the company" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-24)).

## Trying it on a case

Take a home mortgage. On the usual account, you and the bank strike a private bargain. Seen through Center Study, it looks different:

- The loan's value depends on expected future earnings, which depend on property law and courts being there in thirty years.
- That makes the loan a bet on succession: on continuity at the center.
- Inflation, a bailout, or a moratorium are the center deciding where enforcement and forgiveness fall.
- Even if you pay off the mortgage, inflation can still whittle away what you own ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)).

The useful question is never only "can I pay?" It is also "which center backs this credit, and how secure is its succession?"

## Where to read next

- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf) is the full argument, with Desan, Drumm, Bichler and Nitzan, and the derivatives market read as ritual.
- [Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack) is the shortest bridge to Katz's recent work on the state, the juridical and data.

To take it further, pick any public dispute over debt, such as student loans or a sovereign default. Try applying the maxim to it: what in it was *done*, and what merely *happened*? Then ask who is positioned to rule on that distinction.

q: What is an idiom, and what is idiomclining?
a:
## Idiom

In everyday usage an idiom is a fixed phrase whose meaning you can't work out from its words, like "kick the bucket." That is the dictionary sense, not Katz's. Katz takes the word much further, close to its root. He notes that "idiom" means "peculiar," peculiar to oneself, and ultimately "'itself,' which is to say self-same" ([Programming the Same](/post/programming-the-same#p-27)). His working definition is short:

> "An 'idiom,' of course, is a singular use of language, meaningful in its particular and always changing uses" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-7)).

He then makes the strong claim: "There is nothing in language but idioms, so the originary hypothesis is the idiomaticity of idioms" (same paragraph).

**Why this word rather than "theory" or "discourse."** The choice is polemical. Katz says he works with "idiom" "rather than 'theory' or 'knowledge' because I want to defer the possibility of any metalanguage that is not convertible into the language it describes" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-1)). A metalanguage is a privileged vocabulary that claims to stand outside other people's language and judge it: "the bludgeon of the disciplines," as he calls it ([Idiomatic Intelligence as Register](/post/idiomatic-intelligence-as-register#p-14)). If everything is idiom, nobody gets that outside position, Center Study included. The "highest knowledge," he writes, "is to know that you are always in an idiom because there is nothing but idioms" (same paragraph).

**How an idiom ties back to the originary scene.** The root is the scene where language began. In Katz's account, a group of proto-humans converging on a single object had to come up with a sign on the spot that let all of them say, in effect, *we see the same thing, and none of us will grab it*:

> "On the originary scene we see... the creation of an idiom, one which everyone on the scene had to learn on the spot, and which we ourselves relearn in iterating the scene in the originary hypothesis. So, that's it, that's what humans are for—the learning of idioms which is simultaneously their creation." ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-9))

So every idiom repeats that first gesture on a smaller scale. It is a shared way of pointing that lets a particular group say "this is the same." This is why Katz treats an idiom as a kind of measure: "any measure is an idiom, a naming, a labeling, a designation that depends on those who can look at that thing and say 'this is the same,' thereby iterating the fundamental gesture of language" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-4)). It is also why "an idiom implies organization around a center such that there are ever new things to point to at the center and that pointing at those things increases interest in the center" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-8)). A lab's jargon, a family's private jokes, a legal tradition, and Katz's own coinages all fit this description.

**Idioms in terms of grammar.** Center Study breaks language into its elementary speech forms. The *ostensive* points, the *imperative* commands, the *interrogative* asks, and the *declarative* states. In those terms, "an idiom is particular set of ostensive-imperative-interrogative-declarative sequences, so learning an idiom is learning when, for example, someone asking a question or making a statement is really requesting that you do something" ([Scenic/Event Intelligence](/post/scenic-event-intelligence#p-13)). Knowing an idiom means knowing what its sentences actually do to you.

**Insider and outsider.** Idioms are opaque from outside and clear from inside. Katz's revision of information theory measures this: the ideal utterance would be "utterly unintelligible to those not conversant in your idiom and transparent to those who are" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-7)). Yet the more inexhaustible an idiom is, the more translatable it must also be. It has to draw outer circles into itself (p-8). You can watch this in Katz's own maxims, which are built to be repeated: "donate your resentment to the center," or "everyone saying the same thing so that everyone doesn't do the same thing at the same time," which he calls "a pretty close to perfect translation of the results of the originary scene" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-19)). In a single line, that phrase is an idiom compressing the whole hypothesis.

**Against "virality."** Katz contrasts the idiom with "viral" theories of language, the Burroughs line, in which you "catch" a discourse like a cold. He grants these theories "a lot of truth" but says they concede what he will not: "the possibility of deferral" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-6)). An idiom is something you enter and organize. You are not simply infected by it.

## Idiomclining

The word comes from linguistics. *Grammaticalization* is the slow drift by which content words slide down a "cline" (a gradual slope) into grammatical functions. "Take," for example, thins out from a concrete grasping into "take over," "take time," "take on." Years ago Katz coined **upclining** for the reverse motion: "retrieving grammaticized signs and re-semanticizing them," in the Benjaminian sense that a worn-down term holds a memory that might "flash up in a moment of danger" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-16)). In his earlier essay he defines an upcline as a word "deliberately removed from a circulation that splinters its uses, and placed within a new circulation, or idiom, that treats the word as a prompt for a new hierarchy of declaratives, imperatives and ostensives" ([Attentionality and Originary Ethics](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-49)). His prototype is Plato pulling "good" out of its everyday use (a good meal, a good house) and setting it up as *the Good* (same paragraph). This is a "retrieval forward, not a recovery of the identical meaning" (p-43).

*Idiomclining* generalizes upclining. It is the ongoing practice of working inside idioms and setting their frozen pieces moving again:

> "dedicating oneself to setting relatively immobilized 'pieces' of language back into motion seems a good way of thinking about operating within an idiom. You will always be mistaken in doing so, precisely because you'll be violating some convention or expectation, but you also can't go wrong because you present a opportunity for an adjusted response on the part of others" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-17)).

The mistake is part of the method. Throughout Katz's work, new linguistic forms are born from a mistaken use that someone else redeems. Idiomclining deliberately puts you at that productive edge.

**What it replaces.** The essay opens with Goodhart's Law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Katz's example is "critical thinking." Institutions define it by a checklist, the checklist becomes the target, and students learn to tick the boxes. Real learning, he argues, happens "only through a mapping of iterable linguistic moves that would be practiced and articulated mistakenly until a new idiom is created in conversation with the idiom we started with—and neither idiom would find arbitrary, bureaucratic abstractions like 'critical thinking' of any use" (p-3). Hence: "'idiomclining' instead of 'critical thinking' or other bureaucratized categories designed for mass test taking. Idiomclining is the interface between the human and computation" (p-17).

**The stance it asks for.** Two aims pull against each other. You want "to make your idiom both more idiomatic and more transferable" (p-15). You speak so exactly to this person, on this topic, that the two of you share a scene no one else is on. You also speak so that either of you could carry the newly made topic to anyone and generate further idioms. Katz calls this a "stance of semiotic research." The method is conversion and compression: nouns turned into verbs, declaratives traced back to the imperatives they carry, imperatives back to what they point at. The aim is to "deliver up to the central intelligence more and more samples around which researchers can virtually gather and say that this is the same" (p-18).

## An example

Take a word your institution has drained of meaning and turned into a target, such as "engagement" or "wellness." The bureaucratic use treats it as a box to tick. An idiomcliner would ask what scene the word once named. Who had to be pointing at what for anyone to say "this is the same"? What command is tucked inside the statement "students should be engaged"? Then you use the word in a slightly wrong way that brings that scene back. For instance, you speak of "engaging" a text as one engages an opponent or engages gears, and you see whether the people around you pick it up. If they do, a small new idiom has formed. If they don't, their correction tells you something about the idiom you are in.

Katz gives a related everyday case for building an idiom under pressure. In a hostile setting you cannot leave, you might restate every expression of hostility "in literal, atonal indicative sentences": "I understand that you would like to take a break now" ([A Sapir-Katz Hypothesis](/post/a-sapir-katz-hypothesis#p-7)). That is a made idiom whose job is deferral. It turns a rush toward conflict into something said rather than done.

## What to read next

- [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) gives the full argument, including the passage on how to sign on dangerous versus "buffered" scenes, which explains why every utterance should be both improvised and ritual-like.
- [Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning) explains why Katz moved from building a grand transdisciplinary theory to working through idioms, and why the originary hypothesis should act as an "infra" rather than a "meta" language.
- [Attentionality and Originary Ethics: Upclining](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics) is the older, more academic essay where the cline/upcline vocabulary first appears, with the "take" example worked out.

As an exercise, pick one of Katz's own coinages, such as "donate your resentment to the center." Try to say what scene it compresses and what imperative it carries, then try to use it once in a conversation where it doesn't quite fit.

q: Apply Center Study to how AI language models are changing writing.
a:
## The starting point: Katz won't defend a "human core"

The usual first move is to look for something human, such as creativity, consciousness or real feeling, that the machine can't reach. Katz declines that move from the beginning. In his view, every attempt to fence off a human remainder just tells engineers what to automate next. In [Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-14) he says the desire to insist on a human/technological distinction "merely inspires someone to try and automate that distinctively human feature and in the process both give us a new treatment of that feature and create a new one, the human ability to simulate something human in technological form. The human is infrahumaning." He makes the same point more sharply elsewhere: lists of what humans can do and machines can't "merely provide a menu of AI improvements for the next generation of programmers to attempt" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-10)).

The question Center Study asks is therefore not what AI can't do. It asks what automating a given writing practice shows about how that practice was put together all along, and what new practice grows up in the gap the automation leaves.

## Writing was never "your own" in the way we pretend

Center Study begins from mimesis: we learn everything, language included, by imitating others. An LLM is a very large machine for imitation, and that is less foreign to us than it seems. Reviewing Mark Amerika's experiments with GPT-2, Katz asks: "Do we not, as language users, also rely upon "large amounts of human generated data"? What else would we call the commonplaces, formulas, and statistical relations between words... that any speaker or writer depends upon and "feeds back" into?" ([Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-16)). He recalls William Coles shuffling sentences from students' drafts into one paragraph, and the students being unable to find their own sentences in it. Of student writing generally he asks: "Don't they often appear somewhat generated by processes and logics outside of the students' own agency?" ([p-24](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-24)).

So the LLM doesn't bring automation into writing. It makes visible an automation that was already there.

## What exactly gets automated: the "classic prose" non-scene

This is where the more specific Center Study analysis comes in. Following David Olson, Katz treats writing as reported speech that has lost gesture and tone. To make up for that loss, writing develops a "metalanguage of literacy": verbs like *claims*, *suggests* and *assumes*, which do the work a voice and a body did in speech. Its ideal form is "classic prose", where "clear" writing would "place reader and writer on the same scene, seeing the same thing" ([From Novice to Apprentice](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-11)). Katz goes as far as saying that "Clarity essentially means unanimity" ([p-12](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-12)).

Here is my reading, built from those passages. An LLM is extremely good at classic prose. Its summaries and paraphrases are clear, well hedged and smooth, the very standard school has taught for generations. Katz says plainly that these models "will produce adequate summaries and paraphrases that will be hard to distinguish... from student writing" ([p-54](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-54)). What gets automated first is the declarative "non-scene": prose that hides the particular scene it was written on. Katz also says classic prose "involves a forgetting of learning... which the idiom, by twisting our discourse in some way, makes us remember" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-4)). An LLM is that forgetting made into a product.

## What moves into the foreground: the idiom, and scenes layered on scenes

An **idiom**, in Katz's sense, is a singular way of speaking that belongs to a particular scene. It is transparent to the people on that scene and opaque to everyone else. That gives a measure that sets idiom directly against prediction. In [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-7) Katz rewrites information theory so that "the greater the predictability of the sample the more one is within the idiom, with the ideal, maximum information generating utterance being utterly unintelligible to those not conversant in your idiom and transparent to those who are." An LLM gives you, as Katz puts it, a reading of your text in terms of "a kind of 'average' language user", and "the more unpredictable your writing, the more 'interesting' the range of continuations" ([Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-17)). The idiom, then, "is conversant with computation... while remaining one step ahead of and one step behind computation" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-6)).

His prediction for writing follows: humans "would start to value, explore, and experiment with forms of speech easier to distinguish from the products of computation," producing writing "more saturated in various references, idioms, tones," writing that constitutes "archives of conversation operating at various levels, produced within a particular institutional and classroom space" ([From Novice to Apprentice](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-55)). The text becomes scenic again, and openly so.

## The new human work: prompting, labeling, "deeming"

Something more radical is going on too. Once we "think in potential 'prompts,' the GenAI is no longer a simple 'tool' that we are standing outside of and 'using.'... The system is using us as much as we are using it" ([AI and Writing review](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-11)). The writer turns into a trainer, someone who judges outputs. Katz brings this back to the most elementary gesture in his whole framework, the act of saying, together with others, "this is the same": "In our interactions with AIs 'all' that might be left is for humans to say 'it's the same picture,' or it's not, or giving degrees of likeness... This will give us more rigorous and demanding work than we have ever done, and more rewarding too" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-20)).

Where would the irreducible difference lie, then? Not in content. It lies in the speech acts that bind a speaker to a center: promising, praying, **deeming**. "AIs can't 'deem,' or if they do deem, they have been authorized or deemed worthy to do so, by, ultimately, a human... We can't credit a machine's promise" ([Toward a Curriculum](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-12), [p-14](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-14)). Underneath all of this is the founding concept: "All that differentiates us fundamentally from the machines, and for the better, is deferral—the deferral of appropriation" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23)). Deferral here means the gesture at the origin of language, holding back from grabbing the shared object so that a scene can form around it.

## A worked case: the cover letter that "reads like AI"

Katz mentions in passing that employers may grow suspicious of letters that read as AI-generated ([p-55](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-55)). Take that case through the framework. A generic cover letter was always nearly machine-made: it is classic prose aimed at no particular scene, built out of the commonplaces of the genre. Now that a machine can produce it, its value as a sign drops to zero, because it no longer shows that anyone stood on this scene. The letter that works now would bring language from the company's own documents, its people and its situation into the writer's own sentences, so that it shows the writer has *entered a scene* and is answering the center of that scene. Katz's classroom answer has the same shape. He uses "combined" sentences in which students weave a text's phrases into their own syntax and then account for how they joined them, because "so far these models can't work with language from a text within another's language in an effective way" ([p-54](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-54); the assignment is described at [p-38](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-38)).

## The honest limit

Katz doesn't claim this as a permanent safe zone. He admits his AI-proof assignments "will very likely no longer be AI-proof one or two or three new large language models down the road," which makes defending them "a rearguard action" ([AI and Writing review](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-5)). The deeper paradox is that "what enables us to study human practice with increasing resolution is the very thing leading to the disappearance of that practice" ([p-6](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-6)). His response is to keep moving. Keep "continually updat[ing] your vocabularies and idioms in ways that the databases... will not have caught up with" ([Paradox and Post-Dox](/post/paradox-and-post-dox#p-10)), and treat every automation as an occasion of inquiry into how the practice it replaces was made. Writing classrooms "have to be sites of inquiry into language (just as the AIs themselves are products of new modes of inquiry into language)" ([p-54](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz#p-54)).

## Where to read next

- **[From Novice to Apprentice](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz)**: the fullest concrete treatment, with the Olson and classic-prose background, the combined-sentence method, and a real student example.
- **[Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining)**: the theory of idiom as "the interface between the human and computation," and why "critical thinking" as a measurable target is the wrong frame.

**An exercise:** take a paragraph an LLM wrote for you and mark every place where it uses the metalanguage of literacy (*suggests*, *highlights*, *underscores*, *it is important to note*). Then ask, for each one, what particular scene a human writer would have had to stand on to say it, and rewrite one sentence so that its scene shows. Pay attention to what you had to know that the model didn't.

q: Why does succession matter so much for judging a social order?
a:
Katz's answer is short and blunt: "the mode of succession is the most important question for assessing a social order—how is the center transferred from one occupant to the next tells us everything important we need to know about that social order" ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-2)). To see why he would claim that much, you have to start from what the center is and what threatens it.

## The center has to stay the same center

In Center Study every human order is organized around a center. It begins with the object on the originary scene that all desire and none may seize, the gesture of deferral that holds everyone back, and the ritual that repeats that gesture. The basic task of any community is to make sure the center it gathers around tomorrow is the same one it gathered around yesterday. Ritual exists for this. Once a human occupies the center (the "Big Man," then kings, then presidents), the task takes a sharper form. As Katz and Baker put it, "If ritual aims at ensuring that the community practicing it remains the same, then once the center has been usurped by a human figure, the most fundamental rituals are succession rituals" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-48)).

A person dies. A ritual object does not. So the moment one occupant gives way to the next is exactly where the community's sameness is most at risk. This is why Katz calls succession "the umbilical cord linking us to the originary scene" and adds: "Whatever 'good' or 'right' that you might have in mind means nothing if the governor of today is not handing off the reins to the governor of tomorrow" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-2)). Elsewhere he names "the continuity of order in the face of tendencies toward mimetic violence" as "the central human problem" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-3)).

## Succession is where resentment is least contained

Resentment, in this idiom, is always ultimately directed toward the center. While an occupant holds the center, that resentment is framed and can be deferred. At the handoff it is not: "The transfer of power is therefore that moment where both the sanctity of the center and the power it confers is formalized and where resentments toward the center are most 'unbound'" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-55)). Every order has to say something at that moment, which is why Katz observes that "no social order can bear an interim in which the transfer of power is not laid out in steps that can produce consensus that the seat of power remains the same—such steps will be invented retroactively, if need be" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-71)). Theories of legitimacy, constitutions and electoral law are, on this reading, all attempts to answer this one problem.

## Succession reveals who actually rules

The second reason concerns power. If you want to know where sovereignty really lies, ask who picks the next sovereign. Katz says this was where his absolutist thinking started: "the most certain test that power was in fact held was that the sovereign selected his successor. Otherwise, would it not be those who selected the successor who wielded power?" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). The same reasoning applies to rules: "if there is some rule of succession independent of the ruler, then the interpreter of that rule is sovereign" ([The Imperative of the Occupant of the Center](/post/the-imperative-of-the-occupant-of-the-center#p-4)). So succession works as a diagnostic. It shows you whether there is "imperium in imperio," some second power behind the official one. "To embody power is to select your successor—if you're not selecting your successor, your power is conditioned on the approval of those who will" ([A New Model of Power](/post/a-new-model-of-power#p-13)).

This is also why he calls the test "very economical." You don't need a full theory of justice or rights to rank regimes. You need one question: can this order present its succession "as representing a form of continuity that could be traced back with as little question as possible to the origin of the social order itself" ([The Imperative of the Occupant of the Center](/post/the-imperative-of-the-occupant-of-the-center#p-3))?

## It is descriptive, not only prescriptive

Katz insists this is what everyone with authority already does, usually without saying so. Parents want children who will carry on their way of life. A founder wants the company to outlive her. A politician grooms people who will continue his agenda. "If you really want what you say you want, how can you just let it all go after you step off the scene? If you're serious, you must want to pass the baton" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-3)). That is why the test reaches past government: "everywhere, succession is the sign of success... A 'childless' practice is a failure" ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-2)).

## Applying it

Take liberal democracy. In Katz's account, it does not solve succession. It turns the problem into regular rotation: the "outside option" (the rival claimant who could replace a king) is brought inside as the opposing party. Two things follow. First, credit enters the picture: "a healthy, which is to say reliable and predictable credit system is necessary for orderly succession, while, conversely, disrupting the credit system is a good way of interfering with succession" ([Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession#p-6)). Second, continuity has to be supplied off the books. Katz argues this is why intelligence agencies become so powerful: they are "the only way to ensure the continuity or any governance if succession is not directed from the center" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-10)). He also notes how frightening things get "when the mechanisms of transitions in power seem broken," and points to 2020 ([Threading through History](/post/threading-through-history#p-9)).

On a small scale, picture a lab whose director retires with no designated heir. The grant agency, the dean and the senior postdocs then all compete to decide what the lab becomes. You can now see who really held the lab's direction, and it was not only the director.

## His positive proposal

From all this Katz derives "singularized succession in perpetuity": the occupant chooses a successor who will be best able to choose a successor, and so on, and the whole social order is organized to produce and test candidates in public. Schools, communities and the arts are all directed toward that work ([The Imperative of the Occupant of the Center](/post/the-imperative-of-the-occupant-of-the-center#p-6)). He admits this cannot guarantee good rulers. No system can, and he keeps hereditary succession as a fallback (p-11). His claim is that an order which openly treats continuity as "the social problem" ([The Problem of Obedience, Revisited](/post/the-problem-of-obedience-revisited#p-11)) organizes its attention better than one that treats every occupant of the center as a usurper waiting to be removed.

## Read next

- [The Imperative of the Occupant of the Center](/post/the-imperative-of-the-occupant-of-the-center): a short, concrete sketch of how a succession-centered order would train and select rulers, and what kind of character it would produce.
- [Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf): the longer argument linking succession to rights, resentment and the disciplines.

**An exercise:** pick an institution you belong to, such as a workplace, church or club, and ask who actually decides who leads it next. Then compare that with what the institution says about itself. Katz would say the gap between the two is where its real center lies.
